signs: Small dark brown or black spots, about 6-12 mm across, on leaves, stems, and fruit.
Leaf spots look leathery and often show concentric rings; they usually appear on older, lower leaves first.
Fruit spots are sunken and dry, sometimes with a concentric pattern, often near the stem end.
distinguishingQuestions: Do the spots have a target-like pattern of concentric rings?
Did the symptoms start on the older, lower leaves?
Has the crop been through several days of cool, humid, or rainy weather?
approvedActions: Remove and destroy volunteer tomato and potato plants and nightshade weeds, which can carry the fungus between seasons.
Rotate away from tomatoes and potatoes so infected plant debris can break down.
Improve airflow around plants and avoid working among wet leaves, to limit spread.
Early blight is uncommon in dry, hot conditions and treatment is rarely needed; if it is spreading, consult a local agricultural extension worker before using any product.

signs: Water-soaked patches on leaves that enlarge quickly into purple-brown, oily-looking blotches.
A ring of greyish-white mould may be visible on the underside of leaves around the blotches.
Leaves die and infection spreads rapidly to stems and fruit; fruit turn brown but usually stay firm.
distinguishingQuestions: Did the patches appear suddenly and spread very fast?
Has the weather been cool and very humid, or has there been rain or overhead irrigation?
Is there greyish-white mould on the underside of the leaves?
approvedActions: Remove and destroy volunteer tomato and potato plants and nightshade weeds.
Check that transplants are free of disease before planting.
Avoid overhead sprinkler irrigation where possible, because it favours the disease.
Late blight can spread very fast and cause severe losses; contact a local agricultural extension worker immediately if you suspect it.

articles.problem: Fusarium wilt (Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. lycopersici)
signs: Yellowing and wilting of individual branches, sometimes on only one side of the plant (a 'yellow flag' effect).
Infected plants usually die; a dark brown discolouration inside the stem extends well up from the roots.
Symptoms often first appear around the time fruit is sizing.
distinguishingQuestions: Is the yellowing and wilting on one side or one branch rather than the whole plant evenly?
If you cut the stem, is the inside discoloured dark brown?
Did the symptoms begin around the time the fruit was sizing?
approvedActions: Grow tomato varieties with resistance to Fusarium wilt where they are available.
Clean soil from tools and machinery between fields to limit the spread of infested soil.
Rotate out of tomatoes for several years to reduce the fungus in the soil.
Avoid conditions that encourage root-knot nematodes, which can overcome varietal resistance.
Fusarium and Verticillium wilts look similar; confirming between them needs laboratory testing, so consult a local agricultural extension worker.

signs: Tiny (about 1.5 mm) yellowish insects with white wings, mostly on the undersides of leaves; they fly up when the plant is disturbed.
Leaves may yellow and curl; a sticky honeydew can make leaves look shiny or blackened by sooty mould.
Feeding by sweetpotato whitefly can cause fruit to ripen unevenly.
distinguishingQuestions: Do small white insects fly up when you brush against the plant?
Are the undersides of the leaves sticky or coated in a black sooty film?
Have nearby crops such as melons, cotton, or cole crops recently been harvested or declined?
approvedActions: Keep the area around the crop free of weeds and remove crop residues; whiteflies move in from nearby host crops.
Separate and stagger plantings away from other whitefly host crops where possible.
Conserve natural enemies such as parasitic wasps, lacewings, and lady beetles.
Check field edges first, because whiteflies usually build up there; only treat when numbers are high, and consult a local agricultural extension worker about any product.
Whiteflies can transmit tomato yellow leaf curl virus, so controlling them also reduces that risk.

articles.problem: Tomato yellow leaf curl (Tomato yellow leaf curl virus, TYLCV)
signs: Stunted, upright plant growth; plants infected early are severely stunted.
Leaves are small and curl upward, with strong crumpling and yellowing between the veins and at the margins.
Shortened internodes give the plant a bushy, 'bonsai'-like appearance; flowers often drop and fruit production falls sharply.
distinguishingQuestions: Are the leaves small and curled upward, with yellowing between the veins?
Is the plant stunted and bushy with very short spaces between leaves?
Are flowers dropping without setting fruit?
approvedActions: Select tomato varieties with resistance to tomato yellow leaf curl virus where available.
Use virus-free and whitefly-free transplants, and do not move transplants in from areas known to have the virus.
Manage whiteflies, which spread the virus, and consider fine-mesh row covers to protect young plants.
Remove and destroy infected plants when only a few are affected, and manage weeds around the field.
Remove and destroy old crop residue and volunteer plants after harvest to reduce the virus between seasons.
